metadata.title: Global-in-time smoothing effects for Schrödinger equations with inverse-square potentials

claim or remark: the paper later calls it 'a remark after Lemma 2.2', but it is a precise result that the proof of Theorem 1.3 uses, so it is typed claim.

nodes.name: Inhomogeneous Schrödinger equation with potential
nodes.statement: This note is concerned with smoothing properties of the time-dependent Schr\"odinger equation \begin{align} i\partial_t u(t,x)=Hu(t,x)+F(t,x);\quad u(0,x)=\psi(x), \end{align} with given data $\psi\in L^2({\mathbb{R}}^n)$ and $F\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}({\mathbb{R}};L^2({\mathbb{R}}^n))$, where $H=-\Delta+V(x)$ is a Schr\"odinger operator on ${\mathbb{R}}^n$, $n\ge3$, with a real-valued function $V$ which decays at spatial infinity in a suitable sense and has a critical singularity at the origin.
nodes.statement_short: The Cauchy problem $i\partial_t u=Hu+F$, $u(0)=\psi$, with $H=-\Delta+V$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, $n\ge3$, $V$ decaying with a critical singularity at 0.

nodes.name: Inhomogeneous Schrödinger equation (1.1)
nodes.statement: i\partial_t u(t,x)=Hu(t,x)+F(t,x);\quad u(0,x)=\psi(x),
nodes.label: equation

nodes.name: Global-in-time smoothing effect for the free Schrödinger equation
nodes.statement: \norm{\<x\>^{-\rho}|D|^{1/2}e^{it\Delta}\psi}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}}^{1+n})}\le C\norm{\psi}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}}^n)},
nodes.statement_short: Kato smoothing: $\langle x\rangle^{-\rho}|D|^{1/2}e^{it\Delta}\psi\in L^2_{t,x}$ for $\rho>1/2$.
nodes.label: intro_1

nodes.name: Kato–Yajima estimate
nodes.statement_short: Weighted $L^2_{t,x}$ bound for the free flow with weight in $L^n$.
nodes.label: intro_2

nodes.name: Endpoint Strichartz estimate
nodes.statement: \norm{e^{it\Delta}\psi}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}};L^{\frac{2n}{n-2}}({\mathbb{R}}^n))}\le C\norm{\psi}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}}^n)},
nodes.statement_short: Free flow maps $L^2$ into $L^2_tL^{2n/(n-2)}_x$.
nodes.label: intro_3

nodes.name: Schrödinger operator with inverse-square potential $H_a$
nodes.statement: In particular, the Schr\"odinger operator with the inverse-square potential of the form\ $$ H_a=-\Delta+a|x|^{-2},\quad a>-\frac{(n-2)^2}{4}, $$ has attracted increasing attention since it represents a borderline case for the validity of \eqref{intro_1}--\eqref{intro_3} (\cite{Duy,GVV}), where note that $(n-2)^2/4$ is the best constant in Hardy's inequality \begin{align} \frac{(n-2)^2}{4}\int |x|^{-2}|u|^2dx\le \int|\nabla u|^2dx,\quad u\in C_0^\infty({\mathbb{R}}^n). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: $H_a=-\Delta+a|x|^{-2}$, $a>-(n-2)^2/4$, a borderline case; $(n-2)^2/4$ is the sharp Hardy constant.

nodes.name: Hardy's inequality
nodes.statement: \frac{(n-2)^2}{4}\int |x|^{-2}|u|^2dx\le \int|\nabla u|^2dx,\quad u\in C_0^\infty({\mathbb{R}}^n).
nodes.label: Hardy

nodes.name: Smoothing estimate for inverse-square potentials (Bui–D'Ancona–Duong–Li–Ly)
nodes.statement: Let $n\ge3$, $a\ge -(n-2)^2/4+1/4$ and ${\varepsilon}>0$. Then there exists $C_{\varepsilon}>0$ such that for all $\psi\in L^2({\mathbb{R}}^n)$, $e^{-itH_a}\psi$ satisfies \begin{align} \norm{w(|x|)|D|^{1/2}e^{-itH_a}\psi}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}}^{1+n})}\le C_{\varepsilon}\norm{\psi}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}}^n)} \end{align} where $w(r)=r^{({\varepsilon}-1)/2}(1+r^{\varepsilon})^{-1}$.
nodes.origin_citation: Bui, D'Ancona, Duong, Li, Ly 2017, Theorem 1.2
conclusions: there exists $C_{\varepsilon}>0$ such that for all $\psi\in L^2({\mathbb{R}}^n)$, $e^{-itH_a}\psi$ satisfies
nodes.statement_short: Weighted smoothing $w(|x|)|D|^{1/2}e^{-itH_a}\psi\in L^2_{t,x}$ for $a\ge-(n-2)^2/4+1/4$.
nodes.label: theorem_BDDLL

nodes.name: Weighted smoothing estimate (1.6)
nodes.statement: \norm{w(|x|)|D|^{1/2}e^{-itH_a}\psi}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}}^{1+n})}\le C_{\varepsilon}\norm{\psi}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}}^n)}
nodes.label: theorem_BDDLL_1

nodes.name: Smoothing estimate (1.6) for the full range $a>-(n-2)^2/4$
nodes.statement: Then authors raised a question whether \eqref{theorem_BDDLL_1} holds under the condition $a>-(n-2)^2/4$.

nodes.name: Assumption A on the potential $V$
nodes.statement_short: $|x|V\in L^{n,\infty}$, $x\cdot\nabla V\in L^{n/2,\infty}$, and $-\Delta+V$, $-\Delta-V-x\cdot\nabla V$ are bounded below by $-\delta\Delta$.
nodes.label: assumption_A

nodes.name: Form lower bounds (1.7)
nodes.label: assumption_A_1

nodes.name: $L^2$ inner product notation
nodes.statement: Here $\<f,g\>=\int f\overline g dx$ is the inner product in $L^2({\mathbb{R}}^n)$ and $L^{p,q}$ is the Lorentz space (see the end of this section).

nodes.name: Inverse-square potential satisfies Assumption A
nodes.statement: A typical example satisfying Assumption \ref{assumption_A} is the inverse-square potential $V(x)=a|x|^{-2}$ with $a>-(n-2)^2/4$. In this case, it follows from Hardy's inequality \eqref{Hardy} that \eqref{assumption_A_1} is satisfied with $\delta=1-4|a|/(n-2)^2>0$ if $a<0$ or $\delta=1$ if $a\ge0$.

nodes.name: Potentials with $|x|^2V\notin L^\infty$ satisfying Assumption A
nodes.statement: Moreover, Assumption \ref{assumption_A} is general enough to include some potentials such that $|x|^2V\notin L^\infty$. For instance, we let $c_1,c_2>0$, $\alpha\in{\mathbb{R}}^n$ and $\chi\in C^1({\mathbb{R}})$ such that $0\le \chi\le 1$ and $|\chi^{(k)}(t)|\le |t|^{-k-1}$ for $|t|\ge1$. Then $$ V(x)=\frac{-(n-2)^2/4+c_1}{|x|^{2}}-\frac{c_2\chi(|x-\alpha|)}{|x-\alpha|} $$ satisfies Assumption \ref{assumption_A} with $\delta=c_1-c_2(2+\sup|\chi'|)(|\alpha|+1)$ if $$ 0<c_2<\frac{c_1}{(2+\sup|\chi'|)(|\alpha|+1)}. $$
nodes.statement_short: An inverse-square term plus a Coulomb-type term centred at $\alpha$ satisfies Assumption A when $c_2$ is small relative to $c_1$.

nodes.name: Closability of the quadratic form $Q_H$
nodes.statement: Under Assumption \ref{assumption_A}, Hardy's inequality \eqref{Hardy} implies that the sesquilinear form $$Q_H(u,v)=\<(-\Delta+V)u,v\> ,\quad u,v\in C_0^\infty({\mathbb{R}}^n),$$ is symmetric, non-negative and closable such that the domain of its closure $\overline{Q}_H$ satisfies $D(\overline{Q}_H)=\mathcal H^1({\mathbb{R}}^n)$.
conclusions: the sesquilinear form $$Q_H(u,v)=\<(-\Delta+V)u,v\> ,\quad u,v\in C_0^\infty({\mathbb{R}}^n),$$ is symmetric, non-negative and closable such that the domain of its closure $\overline{Q}_H$ satisfies $D(\overline{Q}_H)=\mathcal H^1({\mathbb{R}}^n)$
nodes.statement_short: Under Assumption A, $Q_H$ is symmetric, non-negative, closable with form domain $\mathcal H^1$.

nodes.name: Friedrichs extension $H$ and inhomogeneous propagator $\Gamma_H$
nodes.statement: Let $H$ be the Friedrichs extension of $\overline Q_H$, $e^{-itH}$ the unitary group on $L^2({\mathbb{R}}^n)$ generated by $H$ via Stone's theorem and $\Gamma_H$ the inhomogeneous propagator defined by \begin{align} \Gamma_HF(t)=\int_0^t e^{-i(t-s)H}F(s)ds,\quad F\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}({\mathbb{R}};L^2({\mathbb{R}}^n)). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: $H$ is the Friedrichs extension of $\overline Q_H$, $e^{-itH}$ its unitary group, and $\Gamma_HF(t)=\int_0^te^{-i(t-s)H}F(s)ds$.

nodes.name: Inhomogeneous propagator (1.8)
nodes.statement: \Gamma_HF(t)=\int_0^t e^{-i(t-s)H}F(s)ds,\quad F\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}({\mathbb{R}};L^2({\mathbb{R}}^n)).
nodes.label: inhomogeneous_propagator

nodes.name: Duhamel formula for the mild solution
nodes.statement: Then a unique (mild) solution to the Schr\"odinger equation \eqref{equation} is given by \begin{align} u(t)=e^{-itH}\psi-i\Gamma_HF(t). \end{align}
conclusions: a unique (mild) solution to the Schr\"odinger equation \eqref{equation} is given by

nodes.name: Mild solution formula (1.9)
nodes.statement: u(t)=e^{-itH}\psi-i\Gamma_HF(t).
nodes.label: solution

nodes.name: Muckenhoupt $A_2$ class
nodes.statement: We say that $v(x)$ belongs to the Muckenhoupt $A_2$ class if $v,1/v\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}({\mathbb{R}}^n)$, $v\ge0$ and $$ \Big(\frac{1}{|B|}\int_B v(x)dx\Big)\Big(\frac{1}{|B|}\int_{B}\frac{1}{v(x)}dx\Big)\le C $$ for all ball $B\subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ with some constant $C>0$ independent of $B$.
nodes.statement_short: $v\ge0$ with uniformly bounded product of ball averages of $v$ and $1/v$.

nodes.name: Global-in-time smoothing estimate for $e^{-itH}$ with radial weights
nodes.statement:
Let $n\ge3$, $V$ satisfy Assumption ef{assumption_A} and $w\in L^2({\mathbb{R}})$. Suppose $w(|x|)^2\in A_2$ and, for any $j=1,2,...,n$, there exists $C_j>0$ such that $$ w(|x|)\le C_jw(x_j),\quad x=(x_1,...,x_n)\in {\mathbb{R}}^n. $$ Then there exists $C>0$, independent of $w$, such that $e^{-itH}$ satisfies $$ 
orm{w(|x|)|D|^{1/2}e^{-itH}\psi}_{L^{2}({\mathbb{R}}^{1+n})}\le C
orm{w}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}})}
orm{\psi}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}}^n)},\quad \psi\in L^2({\mathbb{R}}^n). $$
assumptions: $w(|x|)^2\in A_2$ and, for any $j=1,2,...,n$, there exists $C_j>0$ such that $$ w(|x|)\le C_jw(x_j),\quad x=(x_1,...,x_n)\in {\mathbb{R}}^n. $$
conclusions:
there exists $C>0$, independent of $w$, such that $e^{-itH}$ satisfies $$ 
orm{w(|x|)|D|^{1/2}e^{-itH}\psi}_{L^{2}({\mathbb{R}}^{1+n})}\le C
orm{w}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}})}
orm{\psi}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}}^n)},\quad \psi\in L^2({\mathbb{R}}^n). $$
nodes.statement_short: Under Assumption A, $\|w(|x|)|D|^{1/2}e^{-itH}\psi\|_{L^2_{t,x}}\lesssim\|w\|_{L^2}\|\psi\|_{L^2}$ for $A_2$ radial weights $w\in L^2$.
nodes.label: theorem_1

nodes.name: The BDDLL weight fulfils the conditions of Theorem 1.2
nodes.statement: Assuming $0<{\varepsilon}<1$ without loss of generality, it is easy to see that $w(r)=r^{({\varepsilon}-1)/2}(1+r^{\varepsilon})^{-1}$ fulfills the above conditions.

nodes.statement:
Let $n\ge3$, $ho>1/2$ and ${\mathcal{A}},{\mathcal{B}}\in \{\dot{\mathcal{H}}^{-1/2,ho}({\mathbb{R}}^n),\ L^{ rac{2n}{n+2},2}({\mathbb{R}}^n)\}$. Suppose $V$ satisfies Assumption ef{assumption_A}. Then the solution $u$ to \eqref{equation} given by \eqref{solution} satisfies  egin{align} 
orm{u}_{L^{2}({\mathbb{R}};{\mathcal{B}}^*)}\le C
orm{\psi}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}}^n)}+C
orm{F}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}};{\mathcal{A}})} \end{align} for all $\psi\in L^2({\mathbb{R}}^n)$ and $F\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}({\mathbb{R}};L^2({\mathbb{R}}^n)) \cap L^2({\mathbb{R}};{\mathcal{A}})$.
conclusions: the solution $u$ to \eqref{equation} given by \eqref{solution} satisfies

nodes.label: theorem_2

nodes.name: Inhomogeneous smoothing estimate (1.10)
nodes.label: theorem_2_1

nodes.name: Weighted homogeneous Sobolev space $\dot{\mathcal{H}}^{s,\mu}$
nodes.statement: Here $\dot{\mathcal{H}}^{s,\mu}({\mathbb{R}}^n)$ denotes the weighted homogeneous Sobolev space equipped with the norm $\norm{f}_{\dot{\mathcal{H}}^{s,\mu}}=\norm{\<x\>^{\mu}|D|^{s}f}_{L^2}$.

nodes.name: Special cases of Theorem 1.3
nodes.statement: Note that $(L^{\frac{2n}{n+2},2}({\mathbb{R}}^n))^*=L^{\frac{2n}{n-2},2}({\mathbb{R}}^n)$ and $(\dot{\mathcal{H}}^{-1/2,\rho}({\mathbb{R}}^n))^*=\dot{\mathcal{H}}^{1/2,-\rho}({\mathbb{R}}^n)$. If ${\mathcal{A}}={\mathcal{B}}=L^{\frac{2n}{n+2},2}({\mathbb{R}}^n)$, \eqref{theorem_2_1} becomes the endpoint Strichartz estimate and was proved by our previous work \cite{BoMi}. If ${\mathcal{A}}={\mathcal{B}}=\dot{\mathcal{H}}^{-1/2,\rho}({\mathbb{R}}^n)$, \eqref{theorem_2_1} is a generalization of \eqref{intro_1} and seems to be new under Assumption \ref{assumption_A}. Here we stress that ${\mathcal{A}}$ and ${\mathcal{B}}$ do not have to coincide.
nodes.statement_short: For $\mathcal A=\mathcal B=L^{2_*,2}$ (1.10) is the endpoint Strichartz estimate of [BoMi]; for weighted Sobolev spaces it generalizes (1.2).

nodes.name: Notation $L^p_T{\mathcal{X}}$
nodes.statement: For $T>0$ and a Banach space ${\mathcal{X}}$, we denote $\norm{F}_{L^p_T{\mathcal{X}}}=\norm{F}_{L^p([-T,T];{\mathcal{X}})}$.

nodes.name: Lorentz space $L^{p,q}$
nodes.statement:
$L^{p,q}({\mathbb{R}}^n)$ denotes the Lorentz space equipped with the norm $
orm{\cdot}_{L^{p,q}({\mathbb{R}}^n)}$ satisfying $
orm{f}_{L^{p,q}({\mathbb{R}}^n)}\sim
orm{t d_f(t)^{1/p}}_{L^q({\mathbb{R}}_+,t^{-1}dt)}$, where $d_f(t):=\mu(\{x\in {\mathbb{R}}^n\ |\ |f(x)|>t\})$ is the distribution function of $f$.

nodes.name: Abstract setting: Hilbert space, self-adjoint $H$, closed operator $A$
nodes.statement: Let ${\mathcal{H}}$ be a Hilbert space with inner product $\<\cdot,\cdot\>$ and norm $\norm{\cdot}$, $H$ a self-adjoint operator on ${\mathcal{H}}$ and $A$ a densely defined closed operator on ${\mathcal{H}}$.

nodes.name: Resolvent $R_H(z)$
nodes.statement: Let $R_H(z):=(H-z)^{-1}$, $z\notin\sigma(H)$.

nodes.name: $H$-smooth operator (Kato smoothness)
nodes.statement: Then we say that $A$ is {\it $H$-smooth} with bound $a$ if $$ \sup_{z\in {\mathbb{C}}\setminus{\mathbb{R}}}|\<(R_H(z)-R_H(\overline z))A^*\psi,A^*\psi\>|\le \frac{a^2}{2}\norm{\psi}^2,\quad \psi\in D(A^*). $$
nodes.statement_short: $A$ is $H$-smooth with bound $a$ if the imaginary part of the sandwiched resolvent $AR_H(z)A^*$ is uniformly bounded by $a^2/2$.

nodes.name: $H$-supersmooth operator
nodes.statement: We say that $A$ is {\it $H$-supersmooth} with bound $a$ if $$ \sup_{z\in {\mathbb{C}}\setminus{\mathbb{R}}}|\<R_H(z)A^*\psi,A^*\psi\>|\le \frac{a}{2}\norm{\psi}^2,\quad \psi\in D(A^*). $$
nodes.statement_short: $A$ is $H$-supersmooth with bound $a$ if $AR_H(z)A^*$ is uniformly bounded by $a/2$ off the real axis.

nodes.name: Supersmoothness implies smoothness
nodes.statement: Note that if $A$ is $H$-supersmooth with bound $a$ then $A$ is $H$-smooth with bound $(2a)^{1/2}$.

nodes.name: Kato smoothing characterization of (super)smoothness
nodes.statement:
{m (1)} $A$ is $H$-smooth with bound $a$ if and only if, for any $\psi\in {\mathcal{H}}$, $e^{-itH}\psi$ belongs to $D(A)$ for a.e. $t\in {\mathbb{R}}$ and  egin{align} 
orm{Ae^{-itH}\psi}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}};{\mathcal{H}})} \le a
orm{\psi}. \end{align} {m (2)} Suppose $A$ is $H$-supersmooth with bound $a$. Then, for any simple function $F:{\mathbb{R}}	o D(A^*)$ and $t\in {\mathbb{R}}$, $Ae^{-i(t-s)H}A^*F(s)$ is Bochner integrable in $s$ over $[0,t]$ (or $[t,0]$) and satisfies  egin{align}  ignorm{e^{-|{\varepsilon} t|}\int_0^t Ae^{-i(t-s)H}A^*F(s)ds}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}};{\mathcal{H}})}\le a
orm{e^{-|{\varepsilon} t|}F}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}};{\mathcal{H}})} \end{align} for all ${\varepsilon}\in {\mathbb{R}}$. Conversely, if the estimate \eqref{proposition_abstract_1_2} holds for all simple function $F:{\mathbb{R}}	o D(A^*)$ and $|{\varepsilon}|<{\varepsilon}_0$ with some ${\varepsilon}_0>0$, then $A$ is $H$-supersmooth with bound $a$.
conclusions: $A$ is $H$-smooth with bound $a$ if and only if, for any $\psi\in {\mathcal{H}}$, $e^{-itH}\psi$ belongs to $D(A)$ for a.e. $t\in {\mathbb{R}}$ and

if the estimate \eqref{proposition_abstract_1_2} holds for all simple function $F:{\mathbb{R}}\to D(A^*)$ and $|{\varepsilon}|<{\varepsilon}_0$ with some ${\varepsilon}_0>0$, then $A$ is $H$-supersmooth with bound $a$
nodes.statement_short: (1) $H$-smoothness iff $Ae^{-itH}$ is bounded $\mathcal H\to L^2_t\mathcal H$; (2) supersmoothness iff the inhomogeneous estimate for $Ae^{-i(t-s)H}A^*$ holds.
nodes.label: proposition_abstract_1

nodes.name: Homogeneous smoothing estimate (2.1)
nodes.statement: \norm{Ae^{-itH}\psi}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}};{\mathcal{H}})} \le a\norm{\psi}.
nodes.label: proposition_abstract_1_1

nodes.name: Inhomogeneous smoothing estimate (2.2)
nodes.statement: \bignorm{e^{-|{\varepsilon} t|}\int_0^t Ae^{-i(t-s)H}A^*F(s)ds}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}};{\mathcal{H}})}\le a\norm{e^{-|{\varepsilon} t|}F}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}};{\mathcal{H}})}
nodes.label: proposition_abstract_1_2

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.1
nodes.statement: The first statement is due to \cite[Lemma 3.6 and Theorem 5.1]{Kat} (see also \cite[Theorem XIII.25]{ReSi}). The second assertion was proved by \cite[Theorem 2.3]{Dan}.
nodes.statement_short: By citation: part (1) is Kato's theorem, part (2) is D'Ancona's Theorem 2.3.

nodes.name: $H$-smooth operators are infinitesimally $H$-bounded
nodes.statement: Note that if $A$ is $H$-smooth then $A$ is infinitesimally $H$-bounded (\cite[Theorem XIII.22]{ReSi}).

nodes.name: Estimate (2.2) is equivalent to its truncated version (2.3)
nodes.statement: Also note that the estimate \eqref{proposition_abstract_1_2} can be replaced by \begin{align} \bignorm{e^{-|{\varepsilon} t|}\int_0^t Ae^{-i(t-s)H}A^*F(s)ds}_{L^2_T{\mathcal{H}}}\le a\norm{e^{-|{\varepsilon} t|}F}_{L^2_T{\mathcal{H}}}. \end{align}
conclusions: the estimate \eqref{proposition_abstract_1_2} can be replaced by

nodes.name: Truncated inhomogeneous smoothing estimate (2.3)
nodes.statement: \bignorm{e^{-|{\varepsilon} t|}\int_0^t Ae^{-i(t-s)H}A^*F(s)ds}_{L^2_T{\mathcal{H}}}\le a\norm{e^{-|{\varepsilon} t|}F}_{L^2_T{\mathcal{H}}}.
nodes.label: proposition_abstract_1_3

nodes.name: Proof that (2.2) and (2.3) are equivalent
nodes.statement: Indeed, \eqref{proposition_abstract_1_2} implies \eqref{proposition_abstract_1_3} since $s\in [-T,T]$ if $t\in[-T,T]$ and $s\in[0,t]$ (or $s\in [-t,0]$). Conversely, since \eqref{proposition_abstract_1_3} implies $$ \bignorm{e^{-|{\varepsilon} t|}\int_0^t Ae^{-i(t-s)H}A^*F(s)ds}_{L^2_T{\mathcal{H}}}\le a\norm{e^{-|{\varepsilon} t|}F}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}};{\mathcal{H}})} $$ and $a$ is independent of $T$, one has \eqref{proposition_abstract_1_2} by letting $T\to\infty$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.2
nodes.statement:
For the sake of self-containedness, we give the proof for $\Gamma_H$ in detail. The proof for $\Gamma_H^*$ is analogous. Let $\chi\in C_0^\infty({\mathbb{R}})$ be such that $\chi\equiv1$ near $0$ and $0\le\chi\le1$ and set $\chi_{\varepsilon}(t)=\chi({\varepsilon} t)$. Note that $A\Gamma_H\chi_{\varepsilon}(H)=A\chi_{\varepsilon}(H)\Gamma_H$ is well-defined on $L^1_T{\mathcal{H}}$ since $A$ is $H$-bounded. Moreover, the $H$-smoothness of $A$ shows$$ ignorm{Ae^{-itH}\int_{[0,T]}e^{isH}\chi_{\varepsilon}(H)F(s)ds}_{L^2_T{\mathcal{H}}}\le a
orm{F}_{L^1_T{\mathcal{H}}}.$$Using the Christ-Kiselev lemma \cite{ChKi}, one can replace $[0,T]$ by $[0,t]$ in the left hand side to obtain$$
orm{A\chi_{\varepsilon}(H)\Gamma_HF}_{L^2_T{\mathcal{H}}}\le Ca
orm{F}_{L^1_T{\mathcal{H}}}$$with some universal constant $C>0$ independent of $F$. This estimate implies that, for all $F\in L^1_T{\mathcal{H}}$, $A\chi_{\varepsilon}(H)\Gamma_HF$ converges in $L^2_T{\mathcal{H}}$ as ${\varepsilon}	o0$ and the limit denoted by the same symbol $A\Gamma_HF$ satisfies the first estimate in \eqref{lemma_abstract_2_1}. This proves the half part of this lemma. Next, let $F:[-T,T]	o {\mathcal{H}}$ be a simple function. As we have shown, $A\chi_{{\varepsilon}_n}(H)\Gamma_H$ converges to $A\Gamma_HF$ in $L^2_T{\mathcal{H}}$ as $n	o\infty$ for any sequence ${\varepsilon}_n>0$ with ${\varepsilon}_n	o0$. Then one can find a subsequence ${\varepsilon}_{n_k}$ and a null set $\mathcal N\subset [-T,T]$ such that $A\chi_{{\varepsilon}_{n_k}}(H)\Gamma_HF	o A\Gamma_HF(t)$ in ${\mathcal{H}}$ as $k	o\infty$ for all $t\in [-T,T]\setminus \mathcal N$. Hence, in order to show \eqref{lemma_abstract_2_2}, it suffices to check that $$  ignorm{\int_0^tAe^{-i(t-s)H}F(s)ds-A\chi_{{\varepsilon}_{n_k}}(H)\Gamma_HF(t)}_{\mathcal{H}}	o0 $$ as $k	o\infty$ for all $t\in [-T,T]\setminus \mathcal N$. Let us write $F=\sum_{j=1}^N\mathds1_{E_j}(t)f_j$ with $f_j\in {\mathcal{H}}$ and measurable sets $E_j\subset [-T,T]$. Then we have for all $t\in [-T,T]\setminus \mathcal N$,  egin{align*} & ignorm{\int_0^tAe^{-i(t-s)H}F(s)ds-A\chi_{{\varepsilon}_{n_k}}(H)\Gamma_HF(t)}_{\mathcal{H}}\ &\le \sum_{j=1}^N ignorm{\int_{[0,t]\cap M_j}Ae^{isH}(1-\chi_{{\varepsilon}_{n_k}}(H))e^{-itH}f_jds}_{\mathcal{H}}\ &\le \sum_{j=1}^NT^{1/2}\Big(\int_{\mathbb{R}}
orm{Ae^{isH}e^{-itH}(1-\chi_{{\varepsilon}_{n_k}}(H))f_j}_{{\mathcal{H}}}^2ds\Big)^{1/2}\ &\le CT^{1/2}\sum_{j=1}^N
orm{(1-\chi_{{\varepsilon}_{n_k}}(H))f_j}_{{\mathcal{H}}}	o 0 \end{align*} as $k	o\infty$, where we have used H"older's inequality in the third line and the $H$-smoothness of $A$ and the unitarity of $e^{-itH}$ in the last line. This completes the proof.

nodes.statement: Let $\chi\in C_0^\infty({\mathbb{R}})$ be such that $\chi\equiv1$ near $0$ and $0\le\chi\le1$ and set $\chi_{\varepsilon}(t)=\chi({\varepsilon} t)$. As we have shown, $A\chi_{{\varepsilon}_n}(H)\Gamma_H$ converges to $A\Gamma_HF$ in $L^2_T{\mathcal{H}}$ as $n\to\infty$ for any sequence ${\varepsilon}_n>0$ with ${\varepsilon}_n\to0$. Then one can find a subsequence ${\varepsilon}_{n_k}$ and a null set $\mathcal N\subset [-T,T]$ such that $A\chi_{{\varepsilon}_{n_k}}(H)\Gamma_HF\to A\Gamma_HF(t)$ in ${\mathcal{H}}$ as $k\to\infty$ for all $t\in [-T,T]\setminus \mathcal N$.

nodes.statement_short: Obtain identity (2.15).

nodes.name: Dual identity and first bound
nodes.statement_short: Get the dual identity (2.16) and bound (2.15) by (2.8), (2.9).

nodes.name: Reduce to $V_2\Gamma_HF$
nodes.statement: It remains to deal with $\norm{V_2\Gamma_HF}_{L^2_T{\mathcal{H}}}=\sup_{\norm{\widetilde G}_{L^2_T{\mathcal{H}}}=1}|\<\<V_2\Gamma_HF,\widetilde G\>\>_T|$. Since $D(H)$ is dense in ${\mathcal{H}}$, we may assume $\widetilde G(t)\in D(H)$.
nodes.statement_short: Remaining term written by duality against dense $\widetilde G$.

nodes.name: Conclude part (2)
nodes.statement: Then, taking $D(H)\subset D(V_2^*)$ into account, we use \eqref{proof_proposition_abstract_2_3} with $G=V_2^*\widetilde G$, \eqref{proposition_abstract_2_4}, \eqref{proposition_abstract_2_5} and \eqref{proposition_abstract_2_7} to obtain $ |\<\<V_2\Gamma_HF,\widetilde G\>\>_T|\le (s_5+s_4s_7)\norm{F}_{L^2_T{\mathcal{A}}} $ which, together with \eqref{proof_proposition_abstract_2_3}, gives us the second assertion. This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the dual pairing via (2.16), (2.10), (2.11), (2.13).

nodes.name: Proof of (3.5)
nodes.statement:
Let us first consider \eqref{lemma_smoothing_2_1}. When $n=1$, it was proved by \cite{KPV} that $$ \sup_{x\in {\mathbb{R}}}
orm{|D_x|^{1/2}e^{it\partial_x^2}f}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}}_t)}\le C 
orm{f}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}}_x)} $$ which, together with the unitarity of $e^{it\Delta_{\widehat{x}_j}}$ in $L^2({\mathbb{R}}^{n-1})$, implies $$ 
orm{|D_j|^{1/2} e^{it\Delta}\psi}_{L^\infty_{x_j}L^2_TL^2_{\widehat x_j}} \le C
orm{\psi}_{L^2},\quad j=1,2,...,n, $$ uniformly in $T>0$, where $\widehat x_j=(x_1,...,x_{j-1},x_{j+1},...,x_n)\in {\mathbb{R}}^{n-1}$ and $D_j=-i\partial_{x_j}$. \eqref{lemma_smoothing_2_1} then is derived from this estimate as follows. Let $\{C_j(\xi)\}$ be a conical partition of unity on ${\mathbb{R}}^n$ so that $ I=\sum_{j=1}^n C_j(\xi), $ where $C_j\in C^\infty({\mathbb{R}}^n\setminus\{0\})$ such that $\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}
olimits C_j\subset\{2|\xi_j|>|\xi|\}$ and $\partial_\xi^\alpha C_j(\xi)=O(|\xi|^{-|\alpha|})$. If we set $ \wtilde C_j(\xi)=C_j(\xi)|\xi|^{1/2}|\xi_j|^{-1/2} $ then $\wtilde C_j$ also satisfies $\partial_\xi^\alpha C_j(\xi)=O(|\xi|^{-|\alpha|})$ and $ |\xi|^{1/2}=\sum_{j=1}^n\wtilde C_j(\xi)|\xi_j|^{1/2}. $ Since $w(|x|)^2$ belongs to the Muckenhoupt $A_2$-class, $\wtilde C_j(D)$ is bounded on a weighted space $L^2({\mathbb{R}}^n,w(|x|)^2dx)$ by weighted Mikhlin's multiplier theorem (see \cite{KuWh}). Thus we conclude that  egin{align*} 
orm{w(|x|)|D|^{1/2}e^{it\Delta}\psi}_{L^2_TL^2}^2 &\le \sum_{j=1}^n
orm{w(|x|)\wtilde C_j(D)|D_{j}|^{1/2}e^{it\Delta}\psi}_{L^2_TL^2}^2\ &\le C\sum_{j=1}^n
orm{w(|x|)|D_{j}|^{1/2}e^{it\Delta}\psi}_{L^2_TL^2}^2\ &\le C\sum_{j=1}^n
orm{w}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}})}^2
orm{|D_{j}|^{1/2}e^{it\Delta}\psi}_{L^\infty_{x_j}L^2_TL^2_{\widehat x_j}}^2\ &\le C 
orm{w}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}})}^2
orm{\psi}_{L^2}^2 \end{align*} uniformly in $T>0$, where we used the properties $w(|x|)\le C_jw(x_j)$ and $w\in L^2({\mathbb{R}})$ in the third line.
nodes.statement_short: Prove the weighted smoothing estimate (3.5).

nodes.name: One-dimensional smoothing
nodes.statement:
Let us first consider \eqref{lemma_smoothing_2_1}. When $n=1$, it was proved by \cite{KPV} that $$ \sup_{x\in {\mathbb{R}}}
orm{|D_x|^{1/2}e^{it\partial_x^2}f}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}}_t)}\le C 
orm{f}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}}_x)} $$ which, together with the unitarity of $e^{it\Delta_{\widehat{x}_j}}$ in $L^2({\mathbb{R}}^{n-1})$, implies $$ 
orm{|D_j|^{1/2} e^{it\Delta}\psi}_{L^\infty_{x_j}L^2_TL^2_{\widehat x_j}} \le C
orm{\psi}_{L^2},\quad j=1,2,...,n, $$ uniformly in $T>0$, where $\widehat x_j=(x_1,...,x_{j-1},x_{j+1},...,x_n)\in {\mathbb{R}}^{n-1}$ and $D_j=-i\partial_{x_j}$.
nodes.statement_short: Kenig–Ponce–Vega 1D smoothing plus unitarity in the other variables.

nodes.name: Conical partition
nodes.statement: \eqref{lemma_smoothing_2_1} then is derived from this estimate as follows. Let $\{C_j(\xi)\}$ be a conical partition of unity on ${\mathbb{R}}^n$ so that $ I=\sum_{j=1}^n C_j(\xi), $ where $C_j\in C^\infty({\mathbb{R}}^n\setminus\{0\})$ such that $\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}\nolimits C_j\subset\{2|\xi_j|>|\xi|\}$ and $\partial_\xi^\alpha C_j(\xi)=O(|\xi|^{-|\alpha|})$. If we set $ \wtilde C_j(\xi)=C_j(\xi)|\xi|^{1/2}|\xi_j|^{-1/2} $ then $\wtilde C_j$ also satisfies $\partial_\xi^\alpha C_j(\xi)=O(|\xi|^{-|\alpha|})$ and $ |\xi|^{1/2}=\sum_{j=1}^n\wtilde C_j(\xi)|\xi_j|^{1/2}. $
nodes.statement_short: Decompose $|\xi|^{1/2}$ with a conical partition of unity.

nodes.name: Weighted Mikhlin and conclusion
nodes.statement:
Since $w(|x|)^2$ belongs to the Muckenhoupt $A_2$-class, $\wtilde C_j(D)$ is bounded on a weighted space $L^2({\mathbb{R}}^n,w(|x|)^2dx)$ by weighted Mikhlin's multiplier theorem (see \cite{KuWh}). Thus we conclude that  egin{align*} 
orm{w(|x|)|D|^{1/2}e^{it\Delta}\psi}_{L^2_TL^2}^2 &\le \sum_{j=1}^n
orm{w(|x|)\wtilde C_j(D)|D_{j}|^{1/2}e^{it\Delta}\psi}_{L^2_TL^2}^2\ &\le C\sum_{j=1}^n
orm{w(|x|)|D_{j}|^{1/2}e^{it\Delta}\psi}_{L^2_TL^2}^2\ &\le C\sum_{j=1}^n
orm{w}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}})}^2
orm{|D_{j}|^{1/2}e^{it\Delta}\psi}_{L^\infty_{x_j}L^2_TL^2_{\widehat x_j}}^2\ &\le C 
orm{w}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}})}^2
orm{\psi}_{L^2}^2 \end{align*} uniformly in $T>0$, where we used the properties $w(|x|)\le C_jw(x_j)$ and $w\in L^2({\mathbb{R}})$ in the third line.
nodes.statement_short: Weighted Mikhlin multiplier theorem and $w(|x|)\le C_jw(x_j)$ give (3.5).

nodes.name: Proof of (3.6)
nodes.statement_short: Prove (3.6) via a Ionescu–Kenig type estimate with real interpolation.

nodes.name: Reduce to directional estimate
nodes.statement: Next, by the same argument as above, \eqref{lemma_smoothing_2_2} follows from the following estimate \begin{align*} \norm{|D_j|^{1/2}\Gamma_0 F}_{L^\infty_{x_j}L^2_TL^2_{\widehat x_j}} \le C \norm{F}_{L^2_TL^{2_*,2}}. \end{align*} which is a slight generalization of \cite[Lemma 4]{IoKe}, in which the same estimate with $L^{2_*,2}$ replaced by $L^{2_*}$ was proved.
nodes.statement_short: (3.6) follows from a directional inhomogeneous estimate generalizing Ionescu–Kenig.

nodes.name: WLOG $j=1$
nodes.statement: Although the proof is essentially same as that of \cite[Lemma 4]{IoKe}, we briefly recall its strategy for reader's convenience. Without loss of generality, we may assume $j=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the strategy; WLOG $j=1$.

nodes.name: Reduce to $\wtilde\Gamma_0$
nodes.statement: Then it suffices to show \begin{align} \sup_{x_1}\norm{|D_j|^{1/2}\wtilde\Gamma_0 F}_{L^2_TL^2_{\widehat x_1}}\le C\norm{F}_{L^2_TL^{2_*,2}}, \end{align} where $\wtilde \Gamma_0 $ is defined by $$ \wtilde \Gamma_0 F(t):=\int_{-\infty}^te^{i(t-s)\Delta}F(s)ds. $$ Indeed, the corresponding estimate for $\Gamma_0 -\wtilde\Gamma_0 $ follows from \eqref{lemma_smoothing_2_1} and the dual estimate of \eqref{lemma_proof_1_1}.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the retarded propagator $\widetilde\Gamma_0$; the difference is handled by (3.5) and dual Strichartz.

nodes.name: Real interpolation instead of complex
nodes.statement: The only difference from the proof of \cite[Lemma 4]{IoKe} is an interpolation step. While they used the complex interpolation, we will use a real interpolation technique as in \cite[Section 6]{KeTa}.
nodes.statement_short: Use real rather than complex interpolation.

nodes.name: Frequency-sign split
nodes.statement: Let $I_{\pm}=\mathbf1_{\pm}(D_1)|D_1|^{1/2}\wtilde\Gamma_0 $, where $\mathbf 1_\pm(t)=1$ for $\pm t\ge0$ and $\mathbf 1_\pm(t)=0$ for $\mp t\ge0$. It suffices to show that $I_{+}$ is bounded from $L^2_TL^{2_*,2}$ to $L^2_TL^2_{\widehat x_1}$ uniformly in $x_1$ since the proof for $I_{-}$ being analogous.
nodes.statement_short: Define $I_\pm$ and reduce to $I_+$.

nodes.name: $TT^*$ reduction
nodes.statement: By the $TT^*$ argument, $I_{+}\in \mathbb B(L^2_TL^{2_*,2},L^2_TL^2_{\widehat x_1})$ if $I_{+}^*I_{+}$ is bounded from $L^2_TL^{2_*,2}$ to $L^2_TL^{2^*,2}$. Hence, if we define a bilinear form $I$ by$$ I(F,G):=\iint \<I_{+}F(s,\cdot),I_{+}G(t,\cdot)\>dsdt $$ then it suffices to show that \begin{align} |I(F,G)|\le C\norm{F}_{L^2_TL^{2_*,2}}\norm{G}_{L^2_TL^{2_*,2}} \end{align} uniformly in $x_1$ and $T>0$.
nodes.statement_short: $TT^*$ reduces to the bilinear bound (3.13).

nodes.name: Dispersive kernel bound
nodes.statement: It was shown by \cite{IoKe} that $I_{+}^*I_{+}$ is bounded on $L^2({\mathbb{R}}^n)$ and the kernel of $I_{+}^*I_{+}$, denoted by $K_{+}(t,s,x,y)$, satisfies the dispersive estimate: $$ |K_{+}(t,s,x,y)|\le C|t-s|^{-n/2},\quad t\neq s. $$
nodes.statement_short: Ionescu–Kenig dispersive estimate for the kernel of $I_+^*I_+$.

nodes.name: Dyadic decomposition
nodes.statement: We then decompose $I(F,G)$ as $$ I(F,G)=\sum_{k\in{\mathbb{Z}}}I_k(F,G),\ I_k(F,G):=\iint_{t-2^{k+1}}^{t-2^k} \<I_{+}F(s,\cdot),I_{+}G(t,\cdot)\>dsdt. $$
nodes.statement_short: Split $I$ dyadically in $t-s$.

nodes.name: Dyadic bounds
nodes.statement: By using the same argument as in \cite[Lemma 4.1]{KeTa}, we see that \begin{align*} |I_k(F,G)|\le C2^{-k\beta(a,b)}\norm{F}_{L^2_TL^{a'}}\norm{G}_{L^2_TL^{b'}},\quad \beta(a,b)=\frac n2-1-\frac n2(\frac1a-\frac1b) \end{align*} uniformly in $k\in {\mathbb{Z}}$, where $(a,b)$ satisfies one of the following conditions: $$ \text{(i)\ \ $\frac 1a=\frac 1b=0$;\quad (ii)\ \ $\frac{n-1}{2n}\le \frac1a \le \frac12$ and $\frac 1b=\frac12$;\quad (iii)\ \ $\frac{n-1}{2n}\le \frac1b \le \frac12$ and $\frac 1a=\frac12$. } $$ In other words, a vector valued sequence $(I_k)_{k\in {\mathbb{Z}}}$ is bounded from $L^2_TL^{a'}_x\times L^2_TL^{b'}_x$ to $\ell_{\beta(a,b)}^\infty$, where $\ell^p_s=L^p({\mathbb{Z}}, 2^{js}dj)$ is a weighted $\ell^p$ space with the counting measure $dj$.
nodes.statement_short: Keel–Tao bounds for each dyadic piece $I_k$.

nodes.name: Bilinear real interpolation
nodes.statement: Then \eqref{lemma_magnetic_1_3} follows from the technique by \cite[Section 6]{KeTa} based on a bilinear real interpolation.
nodes.statement_short: Bilinear real interpolation yields (3.13).

nodes.name: (3.7) by duality
nodes.statement: The estimate \eqref{lemma_smoothing_2_3} follows from the dual estimate of \eqref{lemma_smoothing_2_2} and H\"older's inequality \eqref{Holder}.
nodes.statement_short: (3.7) from dual of (3.6) and Hölder.

nodes.name: (3.8) by citation
nodes.statement: For \eqref{lemma_smoothing_2_5}, we refer to \cite{Chi}.
nodes.statement_short: (3.8) is due to Chihara.

nodes.statement: \eqref{lemma_smoothing_2_6} and \eqref{lemma_smoothing_2_7} follow from \eqref{lemma_smoothing_2_2} and \eqref{lemma_smoothing_2_3} since $\<x\>^{-\rho}$ satisfies the condition on $w$ in Theorem \ref{theorem_1}.
nodes.statement_short: Specialize (3.6)–(3.7) to $w=\langle x\rangle^{-\rho}$.

nodes.name: Decompose $\Gamma_0$
nodes.statement: In order to derive \eqref{lemma_smoothing_2_8}, we observe from the formula \eqref{adjoint_1} that $\Gamma_0 $ can be brought to the form \begin{align*} \Gamma_0 F(t)=-\Gamma_0 ^*F(t)\pm\Gamma_0 ^{0}F(t)+\Gamma_0 ^{\mp}F(t) \end{align*} for $\pm t\ge0$, where $$ \Gamma_0 ^{0}F(t)=\int_{-T}^Te^{-i(t-s)H}F(s)ds,\quad \Gamma_0 ^{\pm}F(t)=\int_0^{\pm T}e^{-i(t-s)H}F(s)ds. $$
nodes.statement_short: Express $\Gamma_0$ through $\Gamma_0^*$, $\Gamma_0^0$, $\Gamma_0^\mp$.

nodes.name: Conclude (3.11)
nodes.statement: Then the desired estimate for $\Gamma_0 ^*$ is nothing but \eqref{lemma_smoothing_2_6}; the desired estimates for $\Gamma_0 ^{0}$ and $\Gamma_0 ^{\mp}$ follow from \eqref{lemma_proof_1_1}, the dual estimate of \eqref{lemma_smoothing_2_1} with $w=\<x\>^{-\rho}$ and H\"older's inequality \eqref{Holder}.
nodes.statement_short: Bound each piece by earlier estimates.

nodes.name: Factorization and domains
nodes.statement_short: Set $V_1=|x|V$, $V_2=|x|^{-1}$; Sobolev gives the domain inclusions.

nodes.name: $\Delta$-smoothness
nodes.statement: Moreover, \eqref{lemma_proof_1_1} and Proposition \ref{proposition_abstract_1} (1) show that both $V_1$ and $V_2$ are $\Delta$-smooth.
nodes.statement_short: Strichartz plus Prop. 2.1 give $\Delta$-smoothness of $V_1,V_2$.

nodes.name: $H$-smoothing of $V_2$
nodes.statement: On the other hand, Propositions \ref{proposition_abstract_1} and \ref{proposition_smoothing_3} show \begin{align} \norm{V_2e^{-itH}\psi}_{L^2_TL^2}\le C \norm{\psi}_{L^2} \end{align} uniformly in $T>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Supersmoothness of $|x|^{-1}$ gives (3.14).

nodes.name: Apply the abstract theorem
nodes.statement_short: Apply Prop. 2.3 with $H_0=-\Delta$ and the weighted space $\mathcal B$.

nodes.name: Duality
nodes.statement: Then the desired estimate follows from density and duality arguments.
nodes.statement_short: Density and duality.

nodes.name: Bound for $V_2\Gamma_HV_2$
nodes.statement: We use the same decomposition $V=V_1V_2$ as above. Since $V_2$ is $H$-supersmooth, we learn by Proposition \ref{proposition_abstract_1} and a remark after Lemma \ref{lemma_abstract_2} that \begin{align} \norm{V_2\Gamma_HV_2\wtilde G}_{L^2_TL^2}\le C\norm{\wtilde G}_{L^2_TL^2} \end{align} for all simple function $\wtilde G:{\mathbb{R}}\to D(V_2)$ with the constant $C$ independent of $T$ and $\wtilde G$.
nodes.statement_short: Supersmoothness gives (3.15).

nodes.name: Apply the abstract theorem
nodes.statement_short: Apply Prop. 2.3 with the free estimates.

nodes.name: Density
nodes.statement: Then the assertion follows from density of simple functions $F:{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathcal{S}}$ in $L^2_T{\mathcal{A}}$ and $L^2_T{\mathcal{B}}$ and the formula \eqref{solution}.
nodes.statement_short: Density and the Duhamel formula.
